title: Analogy
tagline: Year 1 Foundation — Finding the relationship in one pair and applying it to another

introduction.overview: An analogy question gives a pair of related items and asks you to find another pair with the same relationship. The standard form is A : B :: C : ?, read as "A is to B as C is to ?". The skill is to state the relationship between A and B precisely in one sentence, and then apply that exact sentence to C. Analogies can be word-based, number-based or letter-based.
introduction.placementRelevance: Analogy questions are commonly asked in the reasoning and verbal sections of company aptitude rounds. They are short, but the answer options are often designed to tempt you with a loosely related word, so precision matters.
introduction.realWorldContext: Choosing the right tool for a job, matching a profession with its workplace and recognising that "kilometre is to distance as kilogram is to weight" are everyday uses of analogical thinking.

learningObjectives: State the relationship in a pair in one clear sentence
Recognise the common word-analogy types: worker-tool, worker-product, part-whole, place, young-one, sequence, degree and function
Solve number analogies based on squares, cubes and products
Solve letter analogies based on position shifts
Avoid the trap of a loosely related but wrong option

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Know the squares up to 20² and the cubes up to 10³. For letters, use A = 1, B = 2, … Z = 26 and look at the shift in position.

coreDefinitions: Analogy: a similarity of relationship between two pairs of items.
Relationship sentence: a short sentence that describes how the first item of a pair relates to the second, such as "a doctor works in a hospital".
Worker and workplace: Doctor : Hospital, Teacher : School, Chef : Kitchen.
Worker and tool or product: Carpenter : Furniture, Cobbler : Shoes, Pen : Write.
Part and whole, young one and adult, and degree (hot : scalding) are other common types of relationship.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: The pair in the question defines a rule. The right answer is the option that follows the same rule in the same direction. Reversing the direction (for example Teacher : School versus School : Teacher) breaks the analogy even if the two words are related.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Fill in the blank sentence: "A is the ___ of B." Then check the sentence for the second pair, keeping the order. If it fits naturally, the option is correct; if you have to stretch the sentence, try another option.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Relationship sentence
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Write the exact sentence connecting A and B.
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Bird : Nest → "a bird lives in a nest"; so Bee : Hive

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Worker – tool / product
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: The first item makes or uses the second.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Number – square / cube
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: The second number is a power of the first.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Number – product form
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: The second number is n multiplied by the next number.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Letter shift
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Each letter moves by a fixed number of positions
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Compare each letter of the first word with the corresponding letter of the second.

mainNarrative: Step one is to find the relationship in the first pair. Doctor and Hospital: a doctor works in a hospital. Step two is to apply the same relationship to the third word: a teacher works in a school, so the answer is School and not Library or Market.

Watch the order. In "Cow : Calf :: Dog : ?" the pair goes from the adult to its young one, so the answer is Puppy. An option such as "Wolf" is related to Dog but does not follow the adult-to-young relation.

Number analogies use arithmetic rules. 8 : 64 follows the rule "square of the first", so 9 : 81. If the first pair is 3 : 27, the rule is "cube", so 4 : 64. When a number is not a perfect square or cube, test the n(n + 1) rule: 5 : 30 gives 7 : 56.

Letter analogies work position by position. CAT → DBU: C→D, A→B, T→U, each letter moves one step forward. Apply the same shift to DOG to get EPH. For pair analogies like ACE : FHJ, compute the shift (A to F is +5) and apply it to LNP to get QSU.

deepDiveAspects.title: Degree and intensity analogies
deepDiveAspects.content: Some pairs show increasing intensity, such as Warm : Hot or Pleased : Delighted. The answer must carry the same increase in strength in the same direction.

deepDiveAspects.title: Function analogies
deepDiveAspects.content: Pairs like Thermometer : Temperature or Barometer : Pressure link an instrument to what it measures. If you know the instrument, name its function in one word and test the options for that word.

problemVariations.description: Instrument and what it does or measures.

solvedExamples.title: Worker and workplace
solvedExamples.question: Doctor : Hospital :: Teacher : ?  (Library, School, Market, Home)
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: State the relationship as a sentence and apply it to the third word.

steps.title: State the relationship
steps.explanation: A doctor works in a hospital: worker : workplace.

steps.title: Choose the option
steps.explanation: School is the workplace of a teacher.

solvedExamples.commonTrap: Choosing Library, which a teacher may use, but is not their workplace.

solvedExamples.title: Number analogy
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Test squares, cubes and n(n + 1) in turn.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The second number is the product of the first number and the next integer.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Choosing 49 by assuming "square" after seeing a small number.

solvedExamples.title: Letter analogy
solvedExamples.question: ACE : FHJ :: LNP : ?
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Compare the corresponding letters of the two groups.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Each letter moves five positions forward in the alphabet.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Applying the shift to the first letter only.

shortcutMethods.title: Sentence test

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Look at each option and decide whether it "feels" right.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Write the relationship sentence for the first pair and test it on each option in turn. Only one option makes a sentence that is as accurate as the first.

rulesForApplication: Keep the order of the pair: A : B must match C : D, not D : C.
The relationship must be as specific as in the first pair.
For numbers, try square, cube and n(n + 1) before anything else.
For letters, compare positions letter by letter.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reversing the order of the pair
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Both words are related, so either order seems fine.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Write the sentence in order and check it against the option in the same order.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The word is associated but the relationship is different.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: The relationship must match exactly, not just be "somehow connected".

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Looking for a complex rule when a square or cube fits.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Test squares, cubes and n(n + 1) first.

commonMistakes.mistake: Applying a letter shift to only one letter
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Seeing the first letter move and assuming the rest do.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Check every letter of the first pair.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Eliminate options that have no relationship with the third word at all; then apply the sentence to the rest.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Analogy questions should take under 30 seconds. Skip if the relationship is not clear within 15 seconds and return later.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Precision of the relationship sentence is what separates a correct answer from a tempting wrong one.

summaryBullets: A : B :: C : ? means the same relationship, in the same order.
State the relationship as a sentence.
Letter rules: position shifts, letter by letter.
Do not choose a word that is only loosely related.

keyTakeaways: Define the relationship before looking at the options.
Use arithmetic for number analogies and position shifts for letter analogies.
selfCheckQuestions: Can I solve Cobbler : Shoes :: Carpenter : ?
Can I find the missing number in 3 : 27 :: 4 : ?
Can I continue CAT : DBU :: DOG : ?
